title: Théorie arithmétique. Théorie de Galois des motifs (1965) : notes manuscites (s.d.), tapuscrit (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (inferred from the cote and the NB). The page belongs to Grothendieck's 1965 'Galois theory of motives' reflections. G is an algebraic Q-group acting on a polarized object. A is a finite-dimensional semisimple Q-algebra with a positive involution x ↦ x* (a Rosati-type involution coming from a polarization) and a positive trace. The NB mentions ε: G → G_m and j: G_m → G. These are exactly the 'Tate/weight character' and 'weight cocharacter' later formalized by Saavedra (1972) and Deligne. The argument also needs B to be commutative, so G here should be commutative: an abelian (CM-type) motivic group, or the centre of the motivic Galois group.

Step 1. Let B be the Q-subalgebra of A generated by G(Q). It is commutative and stable under *, and the trace of A restricts to a positive trace on B. By the commutative case of Albert's classification of algebras with positive involution, B is a product of fields L_i. On each factor the involution is either trivial (L_i totally real) or complex conjugation (L_i a CM field). In the CM case K_i = L_i^{*} is the maximal totally real subfield, so it is determined by L_i. The induced trace on each L_i is a positive multiple of Tr_{L_i/Q}.

Step 2. The unit group is B^* = H(Q), with H = ∏_i Res_{L_i/Q} G_m.

Step 3. The unitary group B^{*u} = {x : x x* = 1} is the group of rational points of H^u = ∏_i Res_{K_i/Q} Γ_i. Here Γ_i = ker(N_{L_i/K_i}: Res_{L_i/K_i}G_m → G_m) is the norm-one torus, the quadratic twist of G_m over K_i defined by L_i/K_i.

Step 4. Because each K_i is totally real and L_i/K_i is totally imaginary, H^u(R) is a product of circles U(1). So H^u is an R-anisotropic ('compact') torus. Grothendieck remarks on this peculiarity and apparently wants to deduce a similar compactness for some H^0 (the line is illegible). Presumably this is the part of G modulo weight/Tate twist.

Step 5. The NB proposes to express ε and j in terms of the data on the L_i.

The purpose is to show that the polarization forces the relevant multiplicative-type part of the motivic Galois group, modulo the weight, to be anisotropic over R. This is the germ of the later axiom that a polarizable Tannakian group has a Cartan involution, i.e. is compact modulo weight. It is also the structure of the Serre group / Mumford–Tate groups of CM motives.
errors: The claim that every L_i is a quadratic extension of a totally real K_i omits the factors on which the involution is trivial. Albert's classification also allows totally real factors with L_i = K_i. There the unitary group is μ2 (still 'compact', so the conclusion survives), unless some extra hypothesis, e.g. from the weight, excludes them.

Commutativity of B is needed and is not stated on this page. It holds only if G is commutative (or one works with the centre); for noncommutative G the generated algebra need not be a product of fields.
The conclusion about 'H^0' is cut off and illegible, so the intended statement is incomplete.

ideas.what: Commutative algebra with positive involution and positive trace is a product of totally real and CM fields
Unitary group of a CM algebra is the R-anisotropic torus ∏ Res_{K_i/Q} U(1)_{L_i/K_i}
ideas.modern_name: norm-one torus / compact torus; CM unitary torus

ideas.what: Using polarization positivity to show the motivic Galois group (its multiplicative part modulo weight) is 'compact', with weight cocharacter j: G_m→G and Tate character ε: G→G_m
ideas.modern_name: Polarized Tannakian categories: Cartan involution / compactness modulo weight; Serre group; weight cocharacter
ideas.usually_credited_to: Saavedra Rivano (1972), Deligne–Milne (1982), Serre (1968, Serre group), Deligne (Shimura variety axioms)
ideas.where_published: Ideas transmitted via Saavedra's thesis; Grothendieck's own text unpublished

missed.claim: Documentary evidence that Grothendieck, around 1965, already isolated the anisotropy over R of the multiplicative part of a polarized motivic group via positive involutions. He also already had the weight cocharacter j and the Tate character ε. These are pre-Serre-group, pre-Saavedra formulations of 'compact modulo weight'. Historically interesting for credit, but not mathematically new.
missed.quote: Cela montre en particulier que H^u est un tore "compact" ... (en voilà une particularité!)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It helps date the origin of the polarization ⇒ Cartan involution principle for motivic Galois groups, usually attributed to Saavedra and Deligne.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is standard: Albert classification and CM norm-one tori. Its interest is historical, as an early Grothendieck instance of the compactness-modulo-weight principle for polarized motives, which is generally known to stem from his ideas via Saavedra.
